contentHtml:
Sanjay Desai, Author, Entrepreneur, Founder and CEO, ConsciousLeap, discusses how the Supreme Court’s mental health guidelines are shaping responsibilities for educational institutions and creating a need for preventive mental wellness programmes, trained staff and measurable outcomes

The operations head of a school group with twelve campuses has three vendor proposals on her desk, all sent the week after the Supreme Court’s guidelines were circulated. Each covers the counsellor requirement. Each offers staff training. None explains what happens for the large majority of students who are not in crisis but are not coping well either. She is not short of options. She is short of a way to tell which one will matter.

Those proposals trace back to July 2025. The Supreme Court ruled that mental health sits inside the right to life under Article 21, and it did not stop at the principle. Fifteen guidelines came with it, binding on every school, college and coaching centre, issued under Articles 32 and 141. That matters, because it makes them orders and not advice. The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 had already promised accessible care. Now somebody can be held to it.

Go through the list the way a procurement officer would, and the shopping basket is long. A qualified counsellor or psychologist wherever there are 100 or more students. Tele-MANAS and similar helplines have to be on display where students can see them. Psychological first-aid training for every staff member, teaching or not, twice a year. No more sorting students into batches by marks, no public shaming, no heaping on pressure. Confidential ways to complain, sessions for parents, committees against ragging and harassment, safer hostels. In January 2026 the Court tightened things for higher education, with round-the-clock medical access on residential campuses and yearly reporting of student suicides and unnatural deaths. The Ministry of Education and the UGC are drafting guidelines of their own.

Here is the catch. Almost all of this switches on after a problem has shown itself. A counsellor meets the student who has already come in, a helpline is dialled by someone who is already low, and a grievance process starts once there is a grievance. You could argue that simply having the infrastructure in place counts as prevention, but the guidelines never say so. What they leave out is the stretch before any of this, when a teenager is quietly struggling and has not told anyone yet. For institutions that is a cost to carry, for providers a service to sell, and neither does much to shorten the queue outside the counsellor’s door.

Consider how big that group is. India has more teenagers than any other country, and its youth suicide rate is among the highest in the world. The National Mental Health Survey put the share of 13 to 17 year olds with a diagnosable psychiatric disorder at 7 per cent. That is the visible part. Underneath it sits what NCERT picked up in 2022: 11 per cent of students feeling anxious, 14 per cent describing extreme emotions, and 43 per cent saying their moods swing. Nobody would call that a clinical picture. It is simply what a regular classroom looks like now, shaped by hustle culture, social media, marks, peer pressure, FOMO and the long shadow of COVID, with nobody having shown these students what to do with any of it.

And most of them stay quiet. According to UNICEF and Gallup data from 2021, around 80 per cent of young people with mental health difficulties never ask for help, put off by stigma, by not knowing where to go, or by there being nowhere to go. The trouble does not disappear. It turns up later as lost productivity or substance abuse, and employers and health systems cover the cost. Spending early is cheaper than spending late, which is why NEP 2020, CBSE’s counsellor mandate, Manodarpan and the 2025 ruling all lean the same way.

Ask a school principal what makes compliance hard and the answers are down to earth. Counsellors are scarce outside the cities, so a requirement of one per institution with more than 100 students runs ahead of the people available. A smaller school is told to arrange referrals with outside professionals, and then finds that nobody picks up. There is no agreed way to tell a good provider from a poor one. Fees at many private schools leave little room in the budget. And the bodies meant to monitor all of this are still working out how. The probable outcome is a drawer of compliance certificates and a school day that feels no different to the students.

That is where healthcare and wellness businesses can step in. A school with a protocol on paper but nowhere to send a student needs a hospital or clinic that answers referrals quickly. The twice-yearly training rule is another opening, and a provider whose sessions teachers actually remember, through role plays and follow-ups, will win over one who reads out a slide deck. The long stretch before any crisis is wide open too, and wellbeing and edtech firms can fill it with activity-led sessions inside the timetable. Schools that cannot pay for any of this need CSR money behind them, and state education departments bring a reach that providers lack.

Institutional buyers will increasingly ask a few questions. Does the programme align with UMMEED, Manodarpan and Tele-MANAS? Is confidentiality and data protection built in?

Can outcomes be shown, through engagement, early screening or fewer crisis referrals? Are the people delivering it qualified? Does it support teachers, since an overstretched teacher is poorly placed to notice a struggling student? Providers who can answer plainly will be ahead of those who can only describe their services.

The Court has laid a floor, and it was overdue. What goes on top is still up for grabs, and the providers who work on preventing distress, not just responding to it, will decide a good deal of how this law feels inside a classroom. They will need institutions and policymakers beside them to do it.
